hero.title: Addressing and
hero.text: Build SBD-DHCP01 and its core relay for the workstation VLAN, three single-purpose administration seats in VLAN 60, and directory-enforced limits on where privilege may sign in. Follow the build, explore the dependencies, and keep the evidence.

scene.label: Interactive 3D lesson network showing SBD-DHCP01 leasing addresses to a VLAN 80 test client through the core relay, and the three VLAN 60 administration seats each managing only its own tier.
scene.completeCaption: SBD-DHCP01 leases VLAN 80 addresses through the core relay, and each tier is administered only from its own VLAN 60 seat. Cross-tier sign-ins are refused and logged, and course 1.6 inherits a safe management plane.

nodes.name: SBD-DHCP01
nodes.title: SBD-DHCP01 · 10.0.20.10
nodes.description: Built in lesson 2 in the Servers OU: authorized in the directory, serving the VLAN 80 scope 10.0.80.100–199 through the core relay (F04), and registering client records with a dedicated low-privilege credential. It is Tier 1, managed from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01.

nodes.name: SBD-DC01
nodes.title: SBD-DC01 · 10.0.10.10
nodes.description: One of the two domain controllers from course 1.1 (SBD-DC02 is 10.0.10.11). The scope hands out both as DNS servers, both hold the test client’s secure dynamic DNS record. Both are Tier 0: lesson 3 scopes their Remote Desktop, Windows Remote Management, and AD Web Services rules to AdminJumpBox01 and VLAN 10.

nodes.name: SBD-SUBCA01
nodes.title: SBD-SUBCA01 · 10.0.30.20
nodes.description: The issuing CA from course 1.4, and a Tier 0 system. Lesson 4 moves it, with SBD-PKI-MGMT01, into the Tier 0 Servers OU so the Servers OU’s deny policy never locks Tier 0 out; lesson 6 rescans it to show its hardening survived the move.

nodes.name: TEST CLIENT
nodes.title: Test client · lease from 10.0.80.100–199
nodes.description: A temporary test VM in VLAN 80. It proves the scope, the relay, and secure dynamic DNS registration, then serves as the Tier 2 machine where a Tier 0 sign-in must be refused and logged.

nodes.name: SBD-ADMIN-PC01
nodes.title: SBD-ADMIN-PC01 · 10.0.60.30
nodes.description: The Tier 2 seat: a Windows client in the Admin Workstations OU for endpoint administration (rule A03). In this course it manages the VLAN 80 test client; the fleet arrives in a later course.

nodes.name: SBD-ADMIN-SRV01
nodes.title: SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 · 10.0.60.20
nodes.description: The Tier 1 seat in the Admin Servers OU, for member-server administration such as SBD-DHCP01 (rule A02). The audit custodian’s separate accounts and sessions also start here.

nodes.name: AdminJumpBox01
nodes.title: AdminJumpBox01 · 10.0.60.10
nodes.description: The Tier 0 seat in the Admin Servers OU. Tier 0 accounts manage the domain controllers, SBD-SUBCA01, and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 from here (rule A01), and it is the only seat allowed to reach the core router’s management on VLAN 100.

flows.label: DHCP lease through the core relay (F04)

stepTitles: Define three tiers and map them to OUs
Write the credential rule for each tier
Plan the VLAN 80 DHCP scope and options
Add the permit and deny rows to the register
design.mistake: Placing a system in Tier 1 because it is a member server. SBD-WSUS01 sits in a member-server VLAN, but the part of it that approves the domain controllers’ updates can control Tier 0. Map tiers by what a system controls, not by where it lives.
design.network: Nothing new is built yet. SBD-DC01 and SBD-SUBCA01 run from earlier courses; SBD-DHCP01, the three VLAN 60 seats, and the VLAN 80 test client exist only in the plan.

control.name: Least Privilege
control.body: Least privilege starts on paper: each tier gets its own accounts, its own administration seat, and its own OUs, and the daily account holds no admin rights anywhere. Writing the rule before any host exists gives every later setting a requirement to trace back to.
control.question: Which systems did you place in Tier 0 because of what they control rather than where they sit, and how would you explain that choice to an assessor?

checklist: I mapped each tier to its systems, OUs, admin seat, and accounts, with Tier 0 defined by what it controls.
I wrote the credential rule for each tier and planned separate per-tier accounts for each administrator.
I recorded the VLAN 80 scope plan and the new permit and deny rows, with owners, in the register.

stepTitles: Install and authorize the DHCP role
Create the VLAN 80 scope and its options
Use a dedicated credential for DNS updates
Enable the core relay and pull a test lease
dhcp.mistake: Skipping directory authorization. An unauthorized Windows DHCP server refuses to serve the domain, so no lease arrives and the relay gets blamed. Confirm Get-DhcpServerInDC lists SBD-DHCP01 before you troubleshoot the path.
dhcp.network: SBD-DHCP01 on VLAN 20 now leases an address to the VLAN 80 test client through the core relay (F04) and registers the client’s record with the domain controllers using a dedicated credential.

control.name: Configuration Settings
control.body: Record the scope, options, directory authorization, relay setting, and update credential as configuration decisions tied to the lesson 1 plan. Authorization and the scoped credential are settings with a security reason; write the reason down beside the value.
control.question: If someone started an unauthorized Windows DHCP server in the domain, what would stop it from serving, and how would your records show that?

checklist: I confirmed SBD-DHCP01 is authorized in the directory.
I checked the scope 10.0.80.100–199 and its router, DNS, and domain options against the plan.
I pulled a test lease through the core relay and found the client’s DNS record on both domain controllers.

stepTitles: Create the Admin sub-OUs and link the STIG GPOs
Build the three seats and join them to their sub-OUs
Strip each seat to its tier’s tools
Register each tier’s management paths
Refuse inbound management and scope the DC rules
admin-hosts.mistake: Adding a new, narrower allow rule for AdminJumpBox01 on the domain controllers instead of scoping the existing Remote Desktop, Windows Remote Management, and AD Web Services rules. Allow rules add up, so the broad rules keep accepting any address.
admin-hosts.network: The three administration seats are online in VLAN 60. Management reaches out from them, AdminJumpBox01 to the domain controllers (A01) and SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 to SBD-DHCP01 (A02), and nothing initiates toward them.

control.name: Boundary Protection | Networked Privileged Accesses
control.body: Privileged access now travels through dedicated, managed seats in VLAN 60, one per tier, so every management session starts somewhere controlled and auditable. Registering each path and refusing inbound management on the seats keeps that route the only one.
control.question: Which management paths to the domain controllers were open before you scoped the existing firewall rules, and how did you confirm they are closed now?

checklist: I linked the STIG GPOs to Admin Servers and Admin Workstations before joining the seats, and gpresult shows them applied.
I confirmed each tier’s management ports answer from that tier’s admin seat and that nothing in user space can open a session toward VLAN 60.
I scoped the existing Remote Desktop, Windows Remote Management, and AD Web Services rules on both domain controllers to AdminJumpBox01 and VLAN 10.

stepTitles: Move the Tier 0 servers into their own OU
Deny higher-tier logons on the Servers and Workstations OUs
Deny network logon and record the console exception
Add Tier 0 administrators to Protected Users
Keep one documented break-glass account
Record the multifactor decision and its date
logon-restrictions.mistake: Setting a deny right in the tier logon GPO without repeating the entries course 1.3’s STIG GPO sets for that right. User rights don’t merge across GPOs: the highest-precedence GPO that sets a right wins, so the STIG’s entries for it, such as Domain Admins and Enterprise Admins, quietly drop out.
logon-restrictions.network: The Tier 0 servers have their own OU. AdminJumpBox01 still manages SBD-SUBCA01 after the move, while the Servers and Workstations OUs now refuse Tier 0 sign-ins.

control.name: Access Enforcement
control.body: The deny-logon rights make the directory enforce the tier rule: a Tier 0 credential presented on a lower tier is refused, whoever types it. The console network-logon exception and the break-glass account belong in the enforcement record because each is named, limited, and owned.
control.question: For each exception you recorded, what limits it, who owns it, and what would tell you it was being used outside its purpose?

checklist: I moved SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 into the Tier 0 Servers OU and confirmed Tier 0 can still sign in to them.
I found the Tier 0 group’s SID on the deny lines of the test machine’s user-rights export, and a refused Tier 0 sign-in logged as event 4625 with status 0xC000015B.
I recorded the console network-logon exception, the Protected Users membership, and the break-glass and MFA decisions.

stepTitles: Manage each tier from its own seat
Attempt the forbidden combinations
Renew the test lease under the full rule set
Reconcile the tier matrix with the register
prove.mistake: Keeping only the refusal the user sees. Without event 4625 (status 0xC000015B) on the test client and the router’s deny-log entry for the VLAN 80 session, nothing shows the boundary made the decision.
prove.network: Each tier’s path runs from its own seat: A01 to the domain controller and SBD-SUBCA01, A02 to SBD-DHCP01, A03 to the test client. The lease and DNS update run again under the full rule set; the refused attempts show up in logs, not as paths.

control.name: Audit Record Generation
control.body: The proof rests on records the systems write themselves: events 4624 and 4672 for the permitted sessions, 4625 with status 0xC000015B for the refused sign-in, and the router’s deny log for the blocked VLAN 80 session. Pair each record with what the user saw.
control.question: Which rows of your tier matrix rest on a record the infrastructure wrote, and which still rest only on what you observed?

checklist: I managed each tier from its own seat with its own account and recorded the target’s 4624 and 4672 events.
I captured the user-visible refusal and the matching 4625 event or router deny-log entry for each forbidden attempt.
I renewed the test lease under the full rule set and reconciled the tier matrix with the register.

stepTitles: Baseline the new hosts and rescan the Tier 0 servers
Add this course’s rows to the living records
Put the admin seats first in the quarterly cadence
Write the handoff for course 1.6
scan.mistake: Treating SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 as new hosts. They changed OU, not identity: a rescan compared with their earlier baseline is what shows the move kept their hardening intact.
scan.network: The four new hosts are baselined and the two Tier 0 servers rescanned. The finished management plane stays in view: each seat reaches only its own tier, ready for course 1.6.

control.name: Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning
control.body: New hosts get a first baseline, and changed hosts are rescanned when they change, so an OU move is checked rather than assumed. The privileged seats then move to the front of the quarterly cadence, because drift on the systems that hold Tier 0 sessions costs the most.
control.question: What change to the administration plane would call for a rescan before the next quarter, and who decides?

checklist: I filed first baselines for the four new hosts and rescans of the two Tier 0 servers, with attributed deltas.
I added this course’s decisions to the exception record and its permit and deny rows to the register, with owners.
I wrote the handoff telling course 1.6 that SIEM consoles and collectors are managed only from VLAN 60.
